title: Cookie session versus JWT: pros and cons

videos.script: You sign in to shelf once. On the next request, how does the server know it is still you? {{question}} There are two answers, and this lesson builds both. In the first, the server keeps a row about your login. Your browser holds a random key to that row, in a cookie. {{session}} In the second, the server writes who you are into a token and signs it. Then it keeps nothing at all. That token is a JWT. {{token}} You will take a token apart by hand, and compute its signature yourself. Then you will change one character, and watch the server refuse it. {{signature}} The hard part comes after that. A session ends when its row is deleted. A token cannot be called back. So you will see what short lifetimes, refresh tokens and a denylist cost you. {{revocation}} Along the way you will defend the cookie against requests that other sites start. {{csrf}} And at the end, a table of the trade-offs. For a browser talking to its own API, it points to the cookie. {{choice}}
